title: One-step loss can look perfect while the rollout drifts: training on longer horizons exposes the error that compounds
summary: A model of dy/dt can be trained by asking it to predict the next state from the true current one (one step, or teacher forcing) or by integrating it over many steps from the initial state and comparing the whole path (a rollout). A tiny error per step is invisible in the first loss but compounds in the second, and measurement noise can hide a systematic error that only a long horizon makes visible. A horizon curriculum starts short and grows.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of validation loss against epoch: eight thin blue seed curves, a bold teal mean curve falling from 1 to about 0.055, a dashed amber horizontal noise-floor line at about 0.068 with a shaded band below it.

source.note: Standard theory of multi-step prediction and error propagation. The figure is the design system's synthetic F6.5 render, so no project number is quoted. All numbers were computed for this page for a linear oscillator with a small growth error.

read_the_figure.question: Does the validation loss really fall for every seed, and does it fall below the spread that different seeds already give?
read_the_figure.axes: x: training epoch. y: validation loss on a log scale. Thin lines are separate random seeds, the bold line is their mean, the dashed line marks the seed spread of a baseline.
look_at: The bold mean and the thin curves around it: a mean that falls while individual seeds cross each other is weaker evidence than one where all fall.
The dashed noise-floor line: a gain that ends above it cannot be told from a different random seed.
The slope in the last epochs: still falling means the horizon or the budget limits the result.
Which loss the curve is: a one-step loss and a rollout loss measured on the same run usually differ by orders of magnitude.
read_the_figure.proves: A reported improvement is real only if it is larger than the seed-to-seed spread of the same method; the loss that is plotted must be the one the claim is about.
if_wrong: Showing the best seed or the mean without the spread.
Plotting the training loss when the claim is about held-out rollouts.
A linear vertical axis that hides the last decade of the fall.
must_check: The loss type and horizon of the plotted curve.

terms.meaning: The model starts from each true state in the data and is scored on its prediction one step later.
Feeding the true previous state, not the model's own output, to produce the next prediction.
Integrating the model from the initial state alone, so each step starts from the model's own earlier output.
The number of steps H over which the rollout is compared with the data.
An error made at one step becomes part of the starting state of the next, so it is carried and can grow.
Train with a short horizon first, then lengthen it, so the early gradients are well behaved and the long-range error is finally penalised.
The size of the error a loss has to detect divided by the noise in the data.

remember: One step maps true state to next state: $\Phi_h(y_k)\approx y_{k+1}$. A rollout feeds the output back: $\hat y_{k+1}=\Phi_h(\hat y_k)$.
The error recursion is $e_{k+1}=G_ke_k+\delta_k$ with $G_k$ the Jacobian of the step; if $\|G\|>1$ errors grow geometrically.
For a continuous model, an error $\varepsilon$ in the right-hand side gives a rollout error of at most $\varepsilon(e^{Lt}-1)/L$ (Gronwall).
A rollout loss needs a gradient through many steps, which can vanish or explode as a product of Jacobians.
Chaotic systems limit useful horizons: errors grow like $e^{\lambda_{\max}t}$ regardless of the model.

understand.title: Easy: walking a path with a map that is slightly off
understand.text: Imagine you check each footstep against the true path and correct yourself every time. A tiny sideways error per step never matters. Now walk the whole route with your eyes closed using the same habit: the tiny error adds up and you end far from the path. One-step training grades you with your eyes open; rollout training grades you with your eyes closed.

understand.title: Medium: the error recursion
understand.text: If the model's step differs from the true step by $\delta$ and the true dynamics stretch errors by a factor $G$, the error after $H$ steps is about $\sum_j G^{H-1-j}\delta$. For $G>1$ that is dominated by the last term and equals $\delta\,(G^H-1)/(G-1)$; for $G<1$ it saturates at $\delta/(1-G)$. The same $\delta$ is therefore harmless in a contracting system and fatal in an expanding one.

understand.title: Hard: small errors hide under noise at one step
understand.text: A systematic error of 0.1 percent per step in a model is below a measurement noise of 1 percent, so a one-step loss cannot tell the right model from the wrong one. After 100 steps the same error is 10 percent and stands clearly above the noise. Longer horizons raise the signal, not the noise: that is the statistical argument for rollout training, beyond the simple fact that rollouts are what the model is used for.

understand.title: Hardest: long rollouts are hard to optimise
understand.text: The gradient of a long rollout is a product of step Jacobians. If they stretch, the gradient explodes; if they contract, early steps stop contributing. For stiff or chaotic systems the loss landscape of a long horizon is rugged, and a start with the full horizon often fails. A curriculum grows $H$ so the optimiser first fits the local rate law and only later the global shape, or uses multiple shooting: break the horizon into windows, start each from the data, and add a continuity penalty at the joints.

steps.title: One-step and rollout losses
steps.note: $L_H$ with $H=1$ is the one-step loss. The superscript means the step map applied $j$ times to its own output, so the early error enters every later term.

steps.title: The compounding recursion
steps.note: Linearised around the true path. For constant $G$ and $\delta$ the sum is geometric.

steps.title: Geometric growth or saturation
steps.note: A model whose per-step error is 0.001 reaches 0.105 after 100 steps if the dynamics have growth rate $e^{0.001}$ per step ($e^{0.1}-1$), and 1.72 after 1000 steps (computed below).

steps.title: An oscillator whose model has a growth error
steps.note: The true motion is a circle. The model has a small outward drift $\varepsilon=0.01$. With $h=0.1$ the one-step error is $e^{h\varepsilon}-1=0.00100$ in relative size. After $t=10$, 50 and 100 the radius is 1.105, 1.649 and 2.718 times the right one.

steps.title: Signal against noise as the horizon grows
steps.note: With noise $\sigma=0.01$ the one-step SNR is 0.10 (invisible) and the 100-step SNR is 10.5. At horizons 1, 10, 50 and 100 the signal is 0.0010, 0.0101, 0.0513 and 0.105.

steps.title: Horizon curriculum and multiple shooting
steps.note: Grow the horizon while the loss stays trainable. Multiple shooting restarts every window from data and ties the windows with a penalty $\mu$ so the pieces join up.

worked.title: Can a one-step loss see a growth error of 0.01 in noisy data?
worked.problem: A harmonic oscillator is measured with Gaussian noise of standard deviation $\sigma=0.01$ at step $h=0.1$. A candidate model has an extra growth rate $\varepsilon=0.01$. Compute the relative one-step error, the radius after $t=10,50,100$, and the signal-to-noise ratio for horizons of 1 step and 100 steps.
worked.answer: One step: error 0.1 percent, SNR 0.10, so the loss cannot tell a good model from this one. After 100 steps the SNR is 10.5, and at $t=100$ the radius is 2.72 times too large. The same model is indistinguishable at one step and obviously wrong in a rollout.

analyze.q: A model fits the one-step loss to 1e-6 and its 200-step rollout loss is 3e-1. List two reasons that are consistent with both numbers.
analyze.hint: Growth of errors in the dynamics; a systematic bias smaller than the one-step noise.

analyze.q: Why does a rollout loss on a chaotic system not keep improving as the horizon is increased?
analyze.hint: What grows like $e^{\lambda t}$ even for a perfect model?

analyze.q: The training curve of a rollout loss shows seeds that diverge after epoch 50. What would you change in the training schedule?
analyze.hint: Shorter horizon first, gradient clipping, windows.

evaluate.q: Is it fair to compare a one-step-trained and a rollout-trained model by one-step error?
evaluate.hint: Which model was optimised for that loss?

evaluate.q: A curriculum reaches the same final horizon as direct training and ends at the same loss. Was it worth it?
evaluate.hint: Count time to a given loss and failure rate over seeds.

create: Design an experiment on a damped oscillator that shows when the one-step loss and the 50-step loss disagree about which of two models is better.
Write a horizon schedule (epochs against H) for a system with a fast and a slow time scale, and say how you would detect that a stage failed.
Describe how you would estimate the noise floor of a rollout loss from repeated runs.

checks.q: What is the difference between teacher forcing and a rollout?
checks.hint: Where does each step start from?
checks.answer: In teacher forcing each prediction starts from the true state in the data. In a rollout each prediction starts from the model's own previous output, so earlier errors are carried forward.

checks.q: A step map has a per-step error of 0.002 and a growth factor $G=1.01$. Roughly what is the error after 100 steps?
Why does a longer horizon help detect a small bias under noise?
checks.hint: What scales with $H$, and what does not?
checks.answer: The accumulated bias grows with the horizon while the measurement noise on each point does not, so the ratio of signal to noise increases.

checks.q: A paper shows only one-step errors for a model intended for long simulations. What is missing?
checks.hint: What is the model used for?
checks.answer: The rollout error over the intended horizon on held-out initial conditions, with the seed spread: that is the quantity the use case depends on.

checks.q: How would you build a horizon curriculum for training?
checks.hint: Think of a schedule driven by a validation criterion.
checks.answer: Start with $H=1$, double $H$ whenever the validation rollout loss at the current horizon stops improving, and stop at the target horizon; keep the learning rate reduced at each stage and compare against direct training on equal compute.
